You are a programming expert. 
        You will be provided with a patch used to fix a bug. 
        Based on the commit message and modifications in the patch, you need to analyze the root cause of the bug in detail. 

        Here is the patch content:
        From 8c5f991e6876de001ff11829ceb9894d11c80014 Mon Sep 17 00:00:00 2001
From: Richard West <rwest@mit.edu>
Date: Thu, 7 Jul 2011 14:30:17 -0400
Subject: [PATCH] When changing a species name, update the Chemkin thermo NASA
 polynomials.

This fixes a bug introduced in 7339cc176cc7bbc671f4dec65b2f161d351ea270
in which we rename species using their names from primary thermo libraries,
but the chemkin file ended up with a thermo section containing the old name.
Thanks to @connie for reporting the bug, and apologies from me for introducing.
---
 source/RMG/jing/chem/Species.java | 3 +++
 1 file changed, 3 insertions(+)

diff --git a/source/RMG/jing/chem/Species.java b/source/RMG/jing/chem/Species.java
index 5a5d24bf..76139930 100644
--- a/source/RMG/jing/chem/Species.java
+++ b/source/RMG/jing/chem/Species.java
@@ -881,6 +881,9 @@ public class Species {
 				} else{
 					// use the name from the primary thermo library!
 					spe.setName(spe.getThermoData().getName());
+					// regenerate the chemkin-formatted NASA polynomials (small waste of time) because 
+					// these contain the species name, which we just changed.
+					spe.generateNASAThermoData();
 				}
 			}
         	//spe.ID =
-- 
2.25.1


        
        Provide a response strictly in the following format:
        Root cause:<Root cause>

Root cause: The bug was caused by the failure to update the Chemkin thermo NASA polynomials when a species name was changed. Specifically, the code was renaming species using their names from primary thermo libraries, but it did not regenerate the associated thermo data, which still contained the old species name. This inconsistency led to the Chemkin file having outdated information.
